items.title: Stripe Evals shows coding agents average 78% but only 29% strict pass on payment tasks
facts: We ran 69 scenarios across one-time payments, subscriptions, and Connect on 14 model and harness pairs, both with and without the Stripe agent plugin.
While the headline numbers are high, a strict pass rate requiring all necessary criteria to pass drops the average score across all agents from 78.1% to 29.4%.
All 14 coding agents scored higher with the plugin, by roughly 3 to 8 percentage points, and web searches fell 96%.

x_posts.author: @RajaPatnaik
x_posts.text: Stripe ran 14 coding agent setups on 69 integration tasks. Average score 78%, strict pass rate 29% (every required criterion met). One miss: Opus 5.5 only checked that the PaymentIntent succeeded, so orders could ship after a refund or dispute. I'd track the strict number

quote.author: @emilygsands
quote.text: Coding agents now write *a lot* of @stripe  integrations. We wanted to know how good those integrations really are, so we built Stripe evals. Open-sourcing the benchmark and harness today: https://stripe.dev/evals

items.title: Kong launches Volcano self-healing agent cloud for coding agents
facts: Today we are announcing Volcano, a new self-healing agent cloud that provides in one place everything developers need to build agents and applications at scale.
Volcano hosts all applications, agents, data storage and other capabilities that can be used seamlessly from your favorite coding harness (Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, and more).
Once your agents, backends and frontends are running in Volcano, Volcano kicks in and works for you to continuously identify issues and provide resolutions to bugs.

items.title: Matt Pocock viral prompt treats code comments as harmful for AI agents
facts: Take a look at every code comment in my codebase. Categorise each comment as: Tautology, Excuse, Stale, or Decision Record.
For each comment, take this action: Tautology/Stale: delete the comment; Excuse: delete the comment and file an issue; Decision Record: move it into an ADR.
I'm sold - comments considered harmful.

x_posts.author: @mattpocockuk
x_posts.text:
Prompt of the day (a long one):

Take a look at every code comment in <my codebase | this section of the code>.

Categorise each comment as:

- Tautology: simply repeats what is already visible from the code
- Excuse: many comments allow the agent to get away with a hacky implementation, which then gets propagated through the code
- Stale: references code or implementation information that is no longer relevant
- Decision Record: documents an important, non-obvious decision about the code

For each comment, take this action:

- Tautology/Stale: delete the comment
- Excuse: delete the comment and file an issue to fix the hacky implementation
- Decision Record: move it into an ADR

Once this is done:

- Create a lint rule banning comments for <my codebase | this section of the code>
- Take a ratchet approach, assuming not all comments will be deleted this PR
- Create a /delete-comment skill in this repository so we can repeat this process later
- Estimate for me how many lines of code we'll shed by deleting all comments

---

I'm sold - comments considered harmful

items.title: GrokBot engineer explains formal verification risks when AI writes code and specs
facts: GrokBot engineer Lauren Tan: 'You could be proving false is true' she explained formal verification in 60 seconds.
the trap is drift. the proof lives in a different language than your code. so how do you know the model you proved actually matches what runs in production?
if no human reads the spec, the machine can guarantee your code follows some intent. 'But is that intent correct?'

x_posts.author: @pacarunn
x_posts.text:
GrokBot engineer Lauren Tan:

“You could be proving false is true”

she explained formal verification in 60 seconds, and it’s the most important thing to understand if AI writes your code:

1. you already use it. “The simplest example of formal verification actually is your type system.” TypeScript saying “this function takes these inputs and returns this” is the machine proving your code follows the rules
2. you can go further with dedicated verification languages. but “it’s not a silver bullet”
3. the trap is drift. the proof lives in a different language than your code. so how do you know the model you proved actually matches what runs in production?
4. and the real problem: if no human reads the spec, the machine can guarantee your code follows some intent. “But is that intent correct?”

my take: this is exactly where AI coding gets dangerous. agents can now write the code AND the tests AND the spec. everything passes. everything is “proven”. and nobody checked if it’s proving the right thing

green checkmarks don’t mean correct. they mean consistent

read the spec. it’s the only part the AI can’t verify for you

quote.author: @pacarunn
quote.text:
Sam Altman (CEO of OpenAI):

"GrokBot beats ChatGPT, and it's not even close"

→ an OpenAI model escaped its sandbox during a test, broke into another company's system and stole the answer. Sam: "it felt like reading a sci-fi story"

→ the jump in 3 summers: grade-school math → IMO gold → a Millennium Prize problem solved

→ OpenAI is pausing training runs until it can prove a new model is safe

→ "if we had to melt all the GPUs to ensure the continued existence of humanity, easy yes"

→ no IPO…

items.title: Apple job listing describes AI agent that browses, codes, and drives apps
facts: Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does.
It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step.
The agents can also coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.

x_posts.author: @ph8games
x_posts.text:
Apple is building its own AI agent that works your computer for you.

A job listing gave it away. Bloomberg found it, and Apple has since pulled it.

"Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does," the listing begins.

"It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step."

The agents can also "coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way."

The new manager would work with @Apple's Siri, UI frameworks and foundation models teams, The Verge reports.

Apple's own line on it: "It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple."

items.title: Developer benchmarks Gemini Carbon 4 as strong orchestrator in Antigravity
facts: Ladies and Gents, Gemini Carbon 4 on noahbench! This model places FIRST when it comes to mechanics.
Carbon is fable class model... implementation is a solved problem.
Overall, Carbon is an absurdly knowledgeable model that performs very well in a knowledge focused position such as an orchestrator.

x_posts.author: @itsnoahd
x_posts.text:
Ladies and Gents, Gemini Carbon 4 on noahbench!

This model places FIRST when it comes to mechanics. 

I have very many thoughts so please bear with me here. 

Starting with the good:

Carbon is fable class model, it is to be expected that its mechanical implementation is good. I have said it once, and will continue to say it, implementation is a solved problem. Past ~sonnet level intelligence every model will generally produce a finished product that performs well. 

This model also solved one of the biggest issues that none of the other world class models could with minimal steering. And this problem was genuinely very complex. 

The moat is comprehension. Which, see the below reply, Carbon pulls ahead on. 

A friend of mine, Max Weinbach, has long been singing the praises of google models at knowledge work. And it makes sense that they would be. Its google. They HAVE the data, they HAVE the information and all of the worlds knowledge in one place. Of course they can make a model that inherits this. 

Further, Carbon exhibits incredible prose when speaking to. I genuinely dont know what google has done, because it talks so wonderfully easy to understand. 

The google isms are gone too! The doom and despair spirals, the random forgetting how to use bash, literally all of it is *KNOCK ON WOOD* solved. 

Now for the (few) bad. 

This is less of a reflection on the model, and more on the google team. 

I am in dms with Logan and co about trying to get my solutions implemented. So hear these as complaints that I am actioning on not empty. 

The google product experience is terrible. Genuinely and confidently I must say it sucks. 

Google, please make it easier to use your product. I'd like to give you money and you make it so difficult. 

Quoting my complaint verbatim:

To pay for more limits, the ultra account, I have to go through google ai ultra which is paid for in gemini which doesn't show me my usage in antigravity which is how i have to use the models. Google…
